questions.q: A reporter has notes on a CEO's office: carpet, art, a view, a framed photo, a half-eaten sandwich on a gold-rimmed plate. What does the 'telling detail' approach suggest?
choices: Use all of them to show thoroughness
Use the one that reveals most about the person, and cut the rest
Replace them with an adjective like 'lavish'
Save them all for the kicker
questions.explain: The telling detail is about selection: one concrete particular doing the work of a paragraph.

questions.q: Hersey's 'Hiroshima' opens with a clerk turning to speak to a colleague at the exact minute the bomb fell. How does it create mood?
choices: Through vivid adjectives of horror
Through direct address to the reader
Through a music bed
Through understatement: an ordinary moment fixed precisely in time
questions.explain: Hersey's restraint lets the reader supply the dread.

questions.q: An audio producer has great nat sound of a market, recorded on another day in another town, and wants to put it under an interview. What's the problem?
choices: None; ambient sound is just mood
It's too quiet
Nat sound works as evidence of a place, so relocating it without telling listeners misleads them
It will clash with the music bed
questions.explain: Many news organizations frown on adding or moving sound that wasn't recorded at the scene without disclosure.

questions.q: An interviewee goes silent for three seconds before answering a hard question. What would most audio editors advise?
choices: Cut the silence to keep the pace up
Fill it with music
Leave the pause in; silence on tape carries meaning
Replace it with narration
questions.explain: A real pause can be the most powerful moment on tape; manufacturing one by cutting would be dishonest.

questions.q: The same photo of a crowd can read as a celebration or a riot depending on the words under it. What did Roland Barthes call the caption's job here?
choices: Anchorage
Status detail
The hermeneutic code
The pathetic fallacy
questions.explain: In 'Rhetoric of the Image' (1964) Barthes described the caption as anchoring one of an image's possible meanings.

questions.q: A writer's strongest quote is buried mid-paragraph. Where will it carry most weight?
choices: In the headline
At the start of the next paragraph
In a footnote
At the end of its paragraph, or standing alone
questions.explain: The last line of a paragraph is where the reader pauses, so a quote placed there rings on.

questions.q: A podcast lays an ominous drone under a crime story before any facts are in. What's the ethical concern?
choices: It tells listeners how to feel before the evidence does
It's too long
It breaks the inverted pyramid
There's none; mood is always fine in fact
questions.explain: Music is audio's most openly manipulative tool; the question is whether it serves the story or the producer.

ideas: In true stories, mood made from what was really there is craft, and mood made from what wasn't is fabrication.
A few seconds of sound recorded on location puts a listener in a place faster than any description, and works as evidence.
A news photograph's meaning stays unstable until a caption fixes it.
Leave the silence in: a speaker's pause on tape can say more than the answer.
